Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a fungal disease caused by Venturia inaequalis that affects leaves, fruit, and young twigs. It appears as olive-green to brown spots on leaves and dark, scabby lesions on fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaves
Dark, scabby lesions on fruit surface
Premature leaf drop in severe cases
Distorted or stunted fruit growth
Reduced fruit quality and marketability
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing captan, myclobutanil, or sulfur at bud break
Remove and destroy fallen leaves and infected fruit
Prune trees to improve air circulation
Apply protective fungicides every 7-10 days during wet weather
Use resistant apple varieties when possible
prevention_steps: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties
Maintain proper tree spacing for air circulation
Remove leaf litter in fall to reduce overwintering spores
Avoid overhead irrigation
Monitor weather conditions and apply preventive sprays before rain

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a fungal disease caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa affecting apple fruit, leaves, and branches. It causes fruit to rot and mummify on the tree.
symptoms: Purple spots on leaves that enlarge and turn brown
Frog-eye leaf spot pattern with concentric rings
Fruit develops brown rot starting at blossom end
Infected fruit becomes black and mummified
Cankers on branches with rough, cracked bark
treatment_steps: Remove all mummified fruit from tree and ground
Prune out dead and cankered branches
Apply fungicides containing captan or thiophanate-methyl
Spray at pink bud stage and continue through petal fall
Destroy all pruned material immediately
prevention_steps: Remove mummified fruit and infected wood during dormant season
Prune to improve air circulation and light penetration
Apply dormant season sprays with copper or lime sulfur
Avoid wounding trees during maintenance
Keep orchard floor clean of debris

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is a fungal disease caused by Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae that requires both apple and cedar/juniper trees to complete its life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surface
Small tube-like projections on leaf underside
Premature leaf drop in severe infections
Fruit lesions appearing as slightly raised spots
Reduced tree vigor and fruit production
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing myclobutanil or propiconazole
Spray at green tip, tight cluster, and bloom stages
Continue applications every 7-14 days through wet periods
Remove nearby cedar/juniper trees within 2 miles if possible
Focus on protecting new growth
prevention_steps: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Remove cedar/juniper trees within proximity
Apply preventive fungicide sprays starting at bud break
Monitor nearby cedars for orange gelatinous growths
Maintain tree health through proper fertilization

Apple___healthy.description: Healthy apple leaves show no signs of disease or pest damage. They are vibrant green with normal shape and structure.
symptoms: No symptoms - plant is healthy
treatment_steps: No treatment needed - maintain current care practices

treatment_steps: No treatment needed - maintain current care practices
prevention_steps: Maintain acidic soil pH (4.5-5.5)
Ensure adequate drainage
Mulch with pine bark or sawdust
Monitor for early signs of disease or pests
Prune to maintain air circulation

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on cherry is caused by Podosphaera clandestina, creating white powdery fungal growth on leaves, shoots, and fruit.
symptoms: White powdery coating on leaves and shoots
Leaf curling and distortion
Stunted shoot growth
Premature leaf drop
Reduced fruit quality and tree vigor
treatment_steps: Apply sulfur-based fungicides or potassium bicarbonate
Use systemic fungicides like myclobutanil for severe cases
Spray at first sign of disease and repeat every 7-14 days
Prune infected shoots to improve air circulation
Apply treatments during dry weather
prevention_steps: Plant powdery mildew-resistant varieties
Prune trees to improve air circulation
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Apply preventive fungicide sprays in spring
Remove and destroy infected plant material

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Healthy cherry leaves are deep green with smooth texture and no signs of fungal or bacterial infections.
symptoms: No symptoms - plant is healthy
treatment_steps: No treatment needed - maintain current care practices
prevention_steps: Maintain proper tree spacing for air flow
Prune regularly to remove dead or diseased wood
Apply preventive sprays during critical growth stages
Monitor for early disease symptoms
Ensure proper irrigation and drainage

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is a fungal disease caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis that thrives in warm, humid conditions and can significantly reduce yield.
symptoms: Small rectangular gray to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions aligned between leaf veins
Lesions may merge causing large dead areas
Lower leaves affected first, progressing upward
Severe infections cause premature plant death
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing azoxystrobin or pyraclostrobin
Treat at first sign of disease or preventively
Make 2-3 applications at 14-21 day intervals
Rotate fungicide modes of action to prevent resistance
Remove heavily infected plant debris after harvest
prevention_steps: Plant resistant corn hybrids
Practice crop rotation with non-host crops
Till under corn residue to reduce inoculum
Use wider row spacing to improve air circulation
Monitor fields regularly during humid weather

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is caused by Puccinia sorghi and appears as distinctive rust-colored pustules on corn leaves.
symptoms: Small circular to elongate rust-colored pustules
Pustules on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Pustules may turn dark brown to black as they mature
Heavy infections cause premature leaf drying
Reduced photosynthesis and grain fill
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing triazole or strobilurin compounds
Treat when disease is first observed and conditions favor spread
Repeat applications every 14 days if disease pressure continues
Focus on protecting upper leaves during grain fill
Consider treatment economics based on disease severity
prevention_steps: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids
Monitor fields regularly starting at seedling stage
Avoid late planting which increases disease risk
Ensure balanced nutrition to maintain plant health
Remove volunteer corn plants that may harbor disease

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight is caused by Exserohilum turcicum and can cause significant yield losses in susceptible hybrids under favorable conditions.
symptoms: Long, elliptical gray-green to tan lesions on leaves
Lesions may reach 1-6 inches in length
Lesions have distinct margins and run parallel to leaf veins
Lower leaves infected first, disease moves upward
Severe infections cause complete leaf blighting
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing strobilurin or triazole active ingredients
Begin applications when disease first appears on lower leaves
Make 2-3 applications at 10-14 day intervals
Protect upper leaves during critical grain-filling period
Use high-clearance equipment to avoid crop damage
prevention_steps: Plant hybrids with genetic resistance to northern leaf blight
Rotate away from corn for 1-2 years
Till under crop residue to reduce overwintering inoculum
Avoid continuous corn in the same field
Monitor weather forecasts for extended wet periods

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Healthy corn plants have vibrant green leaves with no lesions, spots, or discoloration, showing normal growth and development.
symptoms: No symptoms - plant is healthy
treatment_steps: No treatment needed - maintain current care practices
prevention_steps: Continue scouting fields regularly
Maintain balanced soil fertility
Ensure adequate soil moisture
Rotate with non-host crops
Use disease-resistant hybrids

Grape___Black_rot.description: Grape black rot is caused by Guignardia bidwellii and can destroy entire grape crops if left unmanaged, especially in humid regions.
symptoms: Reddish-brown circular leaf spots with dark margins
Fruit lesions start as pale circular spots
Infected berries shrivel and turn into hard black mummies
Shoot lesions appear as elongated dark brown areas
Black pycnidia (fungal fruiting bodies) visible in lesions
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing mancozeb, captan, or myclobutanil
Begin sprays at bud break and continue until 6 weeks after bloom
Spray every 7-14 days depending on weather conditions
Remove and destroy all mummified fruit
Prune out infected canes during dormant season
prevention_steps: Remove all mummified berries from vines and ground
Prune vines to improve air circulation
Apply dormant season copper sprays
Keep vineyard floor clean of debris
Plant resistant grape varieties when available

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a complex disease involving multiple fungi that causes decline and death of grapevines, particularly affecting older vines.
symptoms: Tiger-stripe pattern on leaves (yellow bands between veins)
Dried, shriveled berries on affected shoots
Dark staining in wood when canes are cut
Sudden wilting of shoots (apoplexy form)
Gradual vine decline over multiple seasons
treatment_steps: No curative treatment available once established
Remove and destroy severely affected vines
Protect pruning wounds with wound sealants
Minimize vine stress through proper irrigation and nutrition
Prune during dry weather to reduce infection risk
prevention_steps: Use clean, disease-free planting material
Sterilize pruning tools between vines with 10% bleach solution
Make pruning cuts at least 1 inch below diseased wood
Avoid unnecessary wounding of vines
Maintain vine vigor through balanced nutrition

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Isariopsis leaf spot is caused by Pseudocercospora vitis and primarily affects foliage, reducing photosynthetic capacity and vine vigor.
symptoms: Angular brown to black spots on leaves
Spots often bordered by leaf veins
White fungal growth visible on lower leaf surface
Premature defoliation in severe cases
Reduced fruit quality and vine vigor
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing copper, mancozeb, or strobilurins
Begin applications at first sign of disease
Spray every 10-14 days during wet weather
Ensure good spray coverage of lower leaf surfaces
Remove and destroy heavily infected leaves
prevention_steps: Prune vines to improve air circulation and light penetration
Remove leaf litter and debris from vineyard floor
Avoid overhead irrigation
Plant vines with adequate spacing
Monitor vines regularly during humid periods

Grape___healthy.description: Healthy grape leaves are vibrant green with no spots or discoloration, showing vigorous growth and proper vine development.
symptoms: No symptoms - plant is healthy
treatment_steps: No treatment needed - maintain current care practices
prevention_steps: Maintain proper vine training and canopy management
Ensure balanced soil fertility and pH
Provide adequate but not excessive water

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Citrus greening (HLB) is a devastating bacterial disease caused by Candidatus Liberibacter species, spread by Asian citrus psyllid. There is no cure.
symptoms: Yellow shoots with mottled, asymmetric leaf yellowing
Small, lopsided fruit with green bottom half
Bitter, unusable fruit
Premature fruit drop
Progressive tree decline and death within 5-10 years
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy infected trees immediately
Control psyllid vectors with systemic insecticides
Apply nutritional sprays to support tree health
Use antibiotics where legally permitted (limited effectiveness)
Focus on vector control as primary management strategy
prevention_steps: Use certified disease-free nursery stock
Implement aggressive Asian citrus psyllid control program
Scout regularly for psyllids and disease symptoms
Remove infected trees within 30 days of confirmation
Establish physical barriers or isolated growing areas

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola and affects leaves, fruit, and twigs of stone fruits, causing significant economic losses.
symptoms: Small angular dark purple to black spots on leaves
Shot-hole appearance as leaf tissue drops out
Fruit lesions appear as small dark spots with raised margins
Cracked, sunken fruit lesions that allow secondary infections
Twig cankers causing dieback in severe cases
treatment_steps: Apply copper-based bactericides during dormant season
Use oxytetracycline antibiotics during growing season where permitted
Spray every 7-10 days during wet weather
Prune out infected twigs and branches
Remove severely infected trees to prevent spread
prevention_steps: Plant resistant peach varieties
Apply copper sprays at leaf fall and delayed dormant stages
Avoid overhead irrigation
Maintain tree vigor through proper nutrition
Use windbreaks to reduce leaf and fruit wounding

Apply preventive copper sprays in fall and spring
Ensure balanced fertilization

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on peppers is caused by several Xanthomonas species and can cause significant yield losses under warm, humid conditions.
symptoms: Small water-soaked spots on leaves
Spots turn brown with yellow halos
Severe infections cause defoliation
Fruit spots are raised with white halos when young
Fruit lesions become brown, corky, and cracked
treatment_steps: Apply copper-based bactericides at first sign of disease
Use products containing mancozeb for added fungal protection
Spray every 5-7 days during wet weather
Remove and destroy heavily infected plants
Reduce humidity through improved air circulation
prevention_steps: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Practice crop rotation (3+ years away from peppers/tomatoes)
Avoid overhead irrigation or water early in day
Sanitize tools and equipment between plants
Plant resistant varieties when available

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is caused by Alternaria solani and affects potatoes and tomatoes, causing yield losses through defoliation and tuber damage.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target pattern)
Spots appear first on older, lower leaves
Yellow halo may surround lesions
Premature leaf drop starting from bottom of plant
Tuber lesions appear as dark, sunken areas
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin
Begin applications before disease appears or at first sign
Spray every 7-10 days throughout growing season
Ensure good coverage of lower leaves
Remove and destroy severely infected plants
prevention_steps: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes
Practice 3-4 year crop rotation
Avoid overhead irrigation or water in morning
Maintain adequate plant spacing for air flow
Remove volunteer potatoes and nightshade weeds

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight caused by Phytophthora infestans is the most destructive potato disease, capable of destroying entire fields within days under favorable conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown/black
White fuzzy fungal growth on lower leaf surface
Rapid spreading - entire fields can be destroyed in days
Brown, greasy lesions on stems
Tuber rot with reddish-brown dry rot
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or cymoxanil immediately
Use systemic fungicides like metalaxyl for high disease pressure
Spray every 5-7 days during cool, wet weather
Destroy infected plants completely
Kill vines 2 weeks before harvest to protect tubers
prevention_steps: Plant certified late blight-free seed potatoes
Use resistant varieties when available
Monitor weather forecasts for blight-favorable conditions
Scout fields daily during vulnerable periods
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potatoes

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew on squash is caused by Podosphaera xanthii and appears as white powdery growth on leaves, reducing photosynthesis and fruit quality.
symptoms: White powdery fungal growth on upper leaf surfaces
Spots may appear on stems and fruit in severe cases
Affected leaves turn yellow and die prematurely
Reduced plant vigor and fruit production
Fruit may be small or poorly developed

Use systemic fungicides like myclobutanil for severe infections
Spray when first symptoms appear and repeat every 7 days

Provide adequate plant spacing for air circulation
Avoid overhead watering

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch is caused by Diplocarpon earlianum and can reduce strawberry yields through defoliation and weakened plant vigor.
symptoms: Numerous small purple to reddish spots on leaves
Spots have white to gray centers
Spots may merge causing large dead areas
Severely affected leaves appear scorched
Premature leaf death and plant weakening
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing captan, myclobutanil, or pyraclostrobin
Begin sprays in early spring when new growth appears
Continue applications every 7-14 days through harvest
Remove and destroy infected leaves
Renovate beds after harvest to remove diseased foliage
prevention_steps: Plant resistant strawberry varieties
Space plants adequately for air circulation
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering
Remove old leaves after harvest
Apply preventive fungicide sprays in spring

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on tomatoes is caused by Xanthomonas species and can cause significant defoliation and fruit damage, especially in warm, humid climates.
symptoms: Small dark brown spots on leaves with yellow halos
Spots may have greasy appearance
Severe infections cause defoliation
Fruit spots are raised, brown, and may crack
Reduced fruit quality and yield
treatment_steps: Apply copper-based bactericides plus mancozeb
Treat every 5-7 days during wet weather
Remove and destroy heavily infected plants
Avoid working in plants when wet
Use products with multiple modes of action
prevention_steps: Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants
Practice 3-year crop rotation away from nightshades
Avoid overhead irrigation
Stake and prune plants for better air circulation
Disinfect tools between plants

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight caused by Alternaria solani is one of the most common tomato diseases, causing characteristic target-spot lesions.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings (target pattern)
Older leaves affected first
Yellow halo may surround spots
Progressive defoliation from bottom upward
Fruit lesions at stem end with concentric rings
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin
Start applications preventively or at first sign of disease
Spray every 7-10 days throughout season
Remove lower leaves showing symptoms
Improve air circulation through staking and pruning
prevention_steps: Use disease-free transplants
Mulch plants to prevent soil splash
Water at base of plants, not overhead
Stake plants and prune lower branches
Rotate crops (3+ years away from tomatoes/potatoes)

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight caused by Phytophthora infestans can destroy tomato crops within days under cool, wet conditions. This is the same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine.
symptoms: Large water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown
White fuzzy fungal growth on lower leaf surface
Dark brown lesions on stems
Firm brown rot on green and ripe fruit
Entire plants can collapse within days
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or cymoxanil immediately
Use systemic fungicides for severe outbreaks
Spray every 5-7 days during cool, wet weather
Remove and destroy infected plants completely
Do not compost infected material
prevention_steps: Use resistant varieties when available
Monitor weather forecasts for blight-favorable conditions
Start preventive fungicide sprays before disease appears
Provide excellent air circulation through spacing and staking
Scout plants daily during vulnerable periods

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mold is caused by Passalora fulva (formerly Fulvia fulva) and primarily affects tomatoes in greenhouses and high-humidity environments.
symptoms: Pale yellow spots on upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grayish-purple fuzzy growth on lower leaf surface
Spots enlarge and turn brown
Severe infections cause leaf curling and death
Reduced photosynthesis and plant vigor
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil or copper
Improve greenhouse ventilation to reduce humidity
Remove infected leaves promptly
Spray every 7-14 days while conditions favor disease
Ensure good air circulation around plants
prevention_steps: Plant resistant varieties (most modern hybrids)
Maintain greenhouse humidity below 85%
Provide adequate plant spacing and air circulation
Water at base of plants early in day
Ventilate greenhouses to reduce leaf wetness

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by Septoria lycopersici and is one of the most destructive tomato diseases, causing extensive defoliation.
symptoms: Numerous small circular spots with gray centers
Dark brown margins around spots
Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in center of spots
Lower leaves affected first
Rapid defoliation from bottom upward
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper
Begin sprays when first spots appear
Continue applications every 7-10 days
Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Mulch heavily to prevent soil splash
prevention_steps: Use disease-free transplants
Mulch with organic material to prevent splash
Stake and prune plants for air circulation
Remove lower leaves as plants grow
Practice 3-year crop rotation

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny arachnids that feed on plant sap, causing stippling and webbing on leaves, particularly during hot, dry weather.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white stippling on leaves
Fine webbing on underside of leaves and between stems
Bronzing or browning of leaves in severe infestations
Premature leaf drop
Reduced plant vigor and fruit production
treatment_steps: Spray plants with strong water jet to dislodge mites
Apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil
Use miticides like abamectin for severe infestations
Repeat applications every 5-7 days
Release predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) as biological control
prevention_steps: Maintain adequate soil moisture to reduce plant stress
Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen
Monitor plants regularly with hand lens
Encourage beneficial predatory mites
Remove heavily infested leaves or plants

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is caused by Corynespora cassiicola and produces characteristic target-like lesions on tomato leaves, stems, and fruit.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric rings (target pattern)
Spots may have yellow halos
Can affect leaves, stems, and fruit
Severe infections cause defoliation
Fruit spots may have raised, corky texture
treatment_steps: Apply fungicides containing chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or azoxystrobin
Begin applications at first sign of disease
Spray every 7-10 days during wet weather
Remove heavily infected leaves
Improve air circulation through pruning
prevention_steps: Use disease-free transplants and seeds
Provide adequate plant spacing
Stake and prune for better air flow
Avoid overhead irrigation
Practice crop rotation

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is transmitted by whiteflies and can cause complete crop failure. There is no cure for infected plants.
symptoms: Upward curling of leaf margins
Yellowing of leaf edges
Stunted plant growth
Reduced fruit set and size
Flowers drop before setting fruit
treatment_steps: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Control whitefly vectors with insecticides (imidacloprid, pyrethroids)
Use sticky traps to monitor whitefly populations
No treatment for virus once plants are infected
Focus on preventing new infections through vector control
prevention_steps: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato varieties
Use reflective mulches to repel whiteflies
Install insect screening on greenhouse vents
Apply systemic insecticides to transplants
Remove infected plants within days of detection

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is highly contagious and spreads through contact, contaminated tools, and handling of infected plants.
symptoms: Mottled light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaf distortion and fernleaf appearance
Stunted plant growth
Reduced fruit set
Fruit may show yellow blotches or uneven ripening
treatment_steps: No treatment available - virus cannot be cured
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately
Disinfect tools with 10% bleach solution between plants
Wash hands thoroughly before handling healthy plants
Do not use tobacco products around tomatoes (can spread virus)
prevention_steps: Plant virus-resistant varieties
Use certified virus-free seeds and transplants
Disinfect tools and hands between plants
Control aphids that may spread the virus
Remove volunteer tomatoes and solanaceous weeds
